analysis.one_liner: Bans large meatpackers from owning or controlling the hogs they slaughter.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: after two weeks it moved to a House Agriculture subcommittee and died there before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Packers and Stockyards Act of 1921 to make it illegal for a meatpacking company to own, feed, or control hogs for more than 14 days before slaughter. It includes exceptions for farmer-owned cooperatives and small packers, and gives companies two years to sell off hog operations they already own. The aim is to stop big packers from raising their own hogs, which independent hog farmers said squeezed them out of the market.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent hog farmers, who would regain a market for their animals instead of competing against hogs raised inside the packing companies' own operations. Farmer cooperatives and small producer-owned packers are explicitly exempted, so producer-owned processing keeps a legal path.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Independent hog farmers and rural communities

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it unlawful for a packer to own, feed, or control swine intended for slaughter, ending the practice of packing companies raising hogs in their own operations [S3].

Producer cooperatives whose members actively raise the hogs, and small packers slaughtering under 2 percent of the national total, are exempted, keeping farmer-owned and small-scale processing legal [S3].
Packers already in the hog business get a two-year transition period to comply, rather than an abrupt cutoff [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large meatpacking companies that operate their own hog farms and feeding operations would lose that business model. Consumers would face no direct cost, though packers argued vertical integration lowers their costs.

drawbacks.text: Some economists and packers argue that packer-owned hog production lowers slaughter costs and can translate into lower meat prices, so the ban could raise costs for processors and potentially consumers [S1].

The 14-day ownership window and the cooperative and small-packer exceptions create line-drawing problems: packers could still control hogs through contractors and financing arrangements just outside the letter of the ban, limiting its real effect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a specific consolidation practice in one sector, with exemptions designed to protect farmer cooperatives and small operators, so the costs fall narrowly on large packers. The main weakness is that sophisticated contracting arrangements could partially evade a 14-day ownership ban. The bigger problem was that it was never seriously considered: it went to a subcommittee and never advanced.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee, then sent to its livestock subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended with no hearing or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. David Minge introduced the bill on November 10, 1999, and it was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture the same day [S1][S5].
One week later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Livestock and Horticulture, and executive comment was requested from USDA [S5].
No further action was taken before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meatpacking companies that own and control their own hog supplies are better off, because the ban never advanced and their vertically integrated hog operations continued. Independent hog farmers who wanted the practice restricted got nothing.

for.name: Rep. David Minge
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban packer ownership of swine.

for.name: 9 of 10 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the other cosponsor was a Republican.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, sent it to the Livestock and Horticulture subcommittee, and took no further action before the Congress ended.

against.name: Subcommittee on Livestock and Horticulture
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after November 17, 1999, with no hearing or markup recorded.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was nearly all Democratic (9 Democrats and 1 Republican among 10 cosponsors), but no vote ever occurred, so the parties' positions on the merits were never tested.

industries.note: Packers that own, feed, or control their own hog supplies would have to exit those operations within two years. Their control of hog supply is what the ban exists to break up, because it lets packers dictate terms to independent hog farmers.
Family hog farmers would face packers that must buy hogs on the open market rather than supply their own, improving their bargaining position. Small farms in rural areas depend on this market.
The bill explicitly exempts producer cooperatives meeting active-member tests, preserving farmer-owned slaughter and processing as a channel.
